title: Abdul El-Sayed Claps Back at Trump’s Anti-Muslim Attacks: 'Call Me Senator Mohamed'
snippet: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed fired back at Donald Trump's rhetoric at a Grand Rapids rally, declaring that the president can simply call him 'Senator Mohamed' after Election Day.
content:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed delivered a sharp, satirical response to Donald Trump’s escalating anti-Muslim rhetoric this weekend, telling supporters in Grand Rapids that the president will have to get used to addressing him by a new title come November.

"I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name," El-Sayed said during a Sunday campaign rally. He pointedly highlighted Trump's financial ties in the Middle East, adding, "He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity. Doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet. He just seems to have trouble pronouncing it when it’s my name."

Dismissing Trump's insults, El-Sayed quipped to the cheering crowd: "I don’t care how he pronounces my name... Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." If victorious, El-Sayed would make history as the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate.

Escalating Rhetoric on the Campaign Trail

El-Sayed's comments follow a series of aggressive personal attacks from Trump while stumping in Michigan for Republican candidate Rep. Mike Rogers. Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed’s faith, referring to the Detroit-area physician as a "jihadist" and a "terrorist sympathizer," while attempting to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood.

At a Sunday rally for Rogers, Trump went so far as to suggest El-Sayed would require a metal detector to enter the Senate chamber and invoked the memory of Sept. 11 hero Todd Beamer, telling voters Michigan needs to "fight just like Todd did to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol."

GOP Opponent Distances Himself from Trump's Labels

Appearing on NBC’s Meet the Press, Rogers attempted to draw a line between his own campaign messaging and Trump’s harsher slurs. Asked directly by host Kristen Welker whether he agreed with Trump calling El-Sayed a "violent terrorist," Rogers demurred.

"No, I don't," Rogers said. "I've never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul."

However, Rogers continued to push claims linking El-Sayed to radical groups, alleging his opponent receives financial support from organizations tied to Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed, a Michigan native born to Egyptian immigrant parents, has forcefully denied any connection to extremist movements, pushing back against the rhetoric as base-level fearmongering.
